title: Röcken to Weimar: the Parsonage, the Rock at Surlej, and the Long Dusk
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Röcken and Naumburg: The Parsonage Childhood

stops.name: Röcken, the parsonage, the pastor's son
stops.campa: In the low parsonage of Röcken, hard by the twelfth-century church, the village pastor Karl Ludwig Nietzsche's first child is born on the fifteenth of October, the very birthday of King Friedrich Wilhelm IV, for whom the boy is named. The bells that toll for the king's day are said in the house to toll also for him, a coincidence the family reads as a small omen. He is baptized in the font his father tends, watched over by mother, grandmother, and aunts in a house already thick with piety and Lutheran learning.
stops.quote: The good fortune of my existence, its uniqueness perhaps, lies in its fatality: I am, to express it in the form of a riddle, already dead as my father, while as my mother I am still living and becoming old.
stops.quote_source: Ecce Homo, "Why I Am So Wise," §1
suggested_refs: The Nietzsche-Gedenkstätte Röcken, the parsonage and church
The baptismal font of the Röcken church

stops.name: Röcken, the father's death, the fatal fall
stops.campa: Karl Ludwig Nietzsche, ailing since a fall struck his head some months before, dies in the parsonage in his thirty-sixth year, leaving a widow, a boy not yet five, and an infant daughter. The village that had called him a saint among pastors now buries him beneath the church he served. Little Fritz, precocious and grave beyond his years, is said to have known beforehand in a dream that his father would come for him, a boy who from this hour walks, in his own later telling, already half a dead man's shadow.
suggested_refs: Karl Ludwig Nietzsche's grave beneath the Röcken church tower

stops.name: Naumburg, the house at Weingarten, exile from Eden
stops.campa: The parsonage must be vacated for the incoming pastor, and at Easter the widow Franziska removes her two children, her own mother, and two unmarried sisters-in-law to a rented house in Naumburg, on the street called Weingarten. Fritz will call the lost Röcken garden a paradise and Naumburg the world after the fall. Here, among five women and no man, the boy grows solemn, correct, devoted to his prayers, so priestly in bearing that the other boys nickname him 'the little pastor' and bring their disputes to him to judge.
suggested_refs: Nietzsche-Haus, Weingarten 18, Naumburg

stops.name: Naumburg, the little parson among women
stops.campa: At the Domgymnasium and in the household on Weingarten the boy reads and prays with a fervor that troubles no one yet, composes hymns, and weeps real tears reciting scripture aloud to his sister and cousins as though he were already in the pulpit his father left empty. Franziska and the aunts indulge and mold him: correctness, cleanliness, a horror of vulgarity. He is already, without knowing it, gathering the iron discipline that Schulpforta will sharpen and that his own hammer will one day be turned against.
suggested_refs: The Nietzsche family Bible and childhood hymn manuscripts, Weimar archive

segments.name: Schulpforta and Bonn: The Break with the Old God

stops.name: Schulpforta, admission to the Fürstenschule
stops.campa: At fourteen the boy is admitted on scholarship to Schulpforta, the ancient Cistercian cloister-school below Naumburg, harshest and most celebrated of the Saxon Fürstenschulen, the same iron walls that decades before formed Fichte, the goose-boy who became a philosopher. Here Nietzsche drills Greek and Latin among the sons of the Prussian gentry, poor and proud among them, and meets the lifelong friend Paul Deussen. The discipline is monastic, the loneliness deep, but the scholar within the little pastor is being forged.
suggested_refs: Schulpforta cloister and its famous library

stops.name: Schulpforta, confirmed beside Paul Deussen
stops.campa: In the school chapel Nietzsche is confirmed at the side of Paul Deussen, the two boys kneeling together before the altar in the rite that should seal a Lutheran life. He composes music and verse for the occasion in devout sincerity, still the pastor's son who wept over scripture at Naumburg. Within three years the same intellect, trained here to interrogate every text with philological rigor, will turn that rigor on the creed itself; but on this morning the confirmed boy believes he is entering, not leaving, the faith of his fathers.
suggested_refs: Schulpforta chapel

stops.name: Schulpforta, graduation, "Fate and History" behind him
stops.campa: Six years of Schulpforta's Latin verses and Greek meters end in graduation. Already in a school essay of 1862, 'Fate and History,' the eighteen-year-old has argued that historical scholarship has quietly discredited Christianity's central claims, a thought he will not yet speak aloud at home. He leaves Pforta a brilliant philologist and a young man whose faith is a shell going hollow, bound for Bonn to study theology as his mother and dead father's calling still require of him.
suggested_refs: Nietzsche's schoolboy essay "Fatum und Geschichte" (1862)

stops.name: Bonn, theology becomes philology, the Franconia corps
stops.campa: Nietzsche matriculates at Bonn in theology and classical philology together, joins the Franconia fraternity, drinks and duels after the student fashion, and even takes a fencing scar to his nose. But the theology withers within one semester: to his devout mother's fury he abandons it entirely, unable to reconcile David Strauss's Life of Jesus and Feuerbach's demolitions with the creed of Röcken and Weingarten. He follows his teacher Friedrich Ritschl instead, transferring to Leipzig to become wholly a philologist.
stops.quote: If you wish to strive for peace of soul and pleasure, then believe; if you wish to be a devotee of truth, then inquire.
stops.quote_source: Letter to his sister Elisabeth, 11 June 1865
suggested_refs: The Bonn Franconia fraternity house
Nietzsche's dueling scar

stops.name: Leipzig, old Rohn's bookshop, Schopenhauer found
stops.campa: New to Leipzig and following Ritschl, the twenty-one-year-old wanders into old Rohn's second-hand bookshop and picks up, by pure accident, a copy of Schopenhauer's The World as Will and Representation. He carries it home, throws himself onto the sofa, and does not rise until he has devoured all six hundred pages. Every line, he will say, screamed renunciation, denial, resignation: a mirror in which he saw the world, life, and his own mind reflected in terrifying grandeur. Philology has just acquired a rival: philosophy as a way of living dangerously.
stops.quote: Here every line screamed renunciation, denial, resignation, here I saw a mirror in which I caught sight of world, of life, and of my own mind in terrifying grandeur.
stops.quote_source: Autobiographical fragment / letter to Carl von Gersdorff, 1865-66
suggested_refs: First edition of Schopenhauer's Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung

segments.name: Leipzig and Basel: The Youngest Chair

stops.name: Leipzig, Ritschl's seminar, the philological prodigy
stops.campa: Under Ritschl's patronage Nietzsche's essays on Diogenes Laertius and the sources of Theognis mark him at once as the most gifted classicist of his generation. He founds a philological society with fellow students, corresponds intensely with Erwin Rohde and Carl von Gersdorff, and reads Schopenhauer and Kant by night against the grain of positivist philology by day. Ritschl privately calls him a phenomenon; the ordinary path of doctorate, then habilitation, then junior post, is about to be broken for him entirely.
suggested_refs: Nietzsche's student essay on Theognis, University of Leipzig

stops.name: Naumburg, the cavalry, the fall from the saddle
stops.campa: Called to his year of Prussian military service, Nietzsche is posted to a mounted artillery regiment garrisoned near his mother's house at Naumburg. Vaulting into the saddle one March morning he strikes his chest hard against the pommel, tearing two muscles in his left side; he cannot walk unaided for months. The would-be soldier is invalided out on extended sick leave rather than formally discharged, and returns, weakened but relieved, to his books at Leipzig, the body already beginning the long rebellion against the mind that will mark his whole life.
suggested_refs: Photograph of Nietzsche in Prussian artillery uniform, 1868

stops.name: Leipzig, the parlor of the Brockhaus family, first meeting with Wagner
stops.campa: At the house of Hermann Brockhaus, Wagner's brother-in-law, the twenty-four-year-old philologist is introduced to Richard Wagner himself, in Leipzig incognito to visit his sister. The two talk long into the night of Schopenhauer, of German music, of the decadence of the age; Wagner plays passages from the still-unfinished Meistersinger. Nietzsche leaves electrified, certain he has met the living genius Schopenhauer's philosophy had seemed only to prophesy. A friendship that will remake and then unmake him has begun.
stops.quote: I was indescribably happy in those days, when I discovered Wagner!
stops.quote_source: Letter to Elisabeth Nietzsche, recalling 1868, in 1882
suggested_refs: Richard Wagner's manuscript of Die Meistersinger, 1868

stops.name: Basel, the chair at twenty-four
stops.campa: On Ritschl's unqualified recommendation the University of Basel calls Nietzsche, not yet twenty-five, without doctorate or habilitation, to the chair of classical philology; Leipzig hastily awards him an honorary doctorate so the appointment can proceed. He arrives on the nineteenth of April, the youngest man ever to hold a tenured Classics chair, and takes rooms in the old Swiss city on the Rhine. The goose-boy's iron schooling and the philologist's brilliance have together bought him, at an age when most men are still students, a professor's title and a European name.
suggested_refs: University of Basel appointment letter, 1869

stops.name: Tribschen, the first visit to the villa on the lake
stops.campa: Wagner, settled with Cosima at the villa of Tribschen above Lake Lucerne, has invited the young professor to visit; Nietzsche overcomes his nerves and takes the boat across on the twenty-fifth of May. It is the first of twenty-three pilgrimages he will make there over three years: weekends of music, talk, and worship at the feet of the man he takes for a second Schopenhauer made flesh. Cosima manages the household and the philosophical conversation alike; the child Siegfried is not yet born. Tribschen becomes, for Nietzsche, the one true home of his adult life.
suggested_refs: Villa Tribschen, now the Richard Wagner Museum, Lucerne

stops.name: Basel, the inaugural lecture: Homer and Classical Philology
stops.campa: Three days after his first Tribschen visit, Nietzsche formally takes up his chair with the inaugural lecture 'On the Personality of Homer,' printed as Homer and Classical Philology. He argues that philology at present holds no clear or consistent idea of itself, and treats it not as dry science but as the handmaid of art and life. The Basel faculty, expecting a cautious junior colleague, hears instead the first note of a young man who will spend his whole career quarreling with his own discipline.
stops.quote: At the present day no clear and consistent opinion seems to be held regarding Classical Philology.
stops.quote_source: Homer and Classical Philology, inaugural lecture, 28 May 1869
suggested_refs: Homer und die klassische Philologie, first printing, 1869

stops.name: Erlangen, the field hospital and the fevers of war
stops.campa: When the Franco-Prussian War breaks out, Nietzsche, a Basel civilian, obtains leave to serve as a volunteer medical orderly. Attending the wounded from Wörth and Weissenburg he is carried in a cattle-truck full of dying men for days, and contracts both dysentery and diphtheria himself. He recovers, gravely weakened, at his uncle's house in Erlangen, then returns to teaching at Basel a changed man: his health, never robust, now permanently undermined, though his intellect, tempered by the sight of mass slaughter, burns only more intensely.
suggested_refs: Nietzsche's war diary fragments, 1870

stops.name: Basel, Die Geburt der Tragödie is published
stops.campa: The Birth of Tragedy out of the Spirit of Music appears, dedicated to Wagner: Nietzsche's first book, half philology and half prophecy, arguing that Greek tragedy was born from the marriage of Apollonian form and Dionysian frenzy, and that Wagner's music-drama is that marriage reborn for the modern age. The professional philologists are scandalized at a colleague writing metaphysics dressed as scholarship; Wilamowitz publishes a savage refutation. Wagner alone is delighted. The book will outlast every review written against it.
suggested_refs: First edition of Die Geburt der Tragödie, 1872

segments.name: Bayreuth and the Breaking of the Idol

stops.name: Bayreuth, laying the foundation stone
stops.campa: On Wagner's fifty-ninth birthday, under dark and rainy skies, the foundation stone of the Festspielhaus is laid on the hill above Bayreuth, the theater that will finally house the Ring cycle as Wagner has always imagined it. Nietzsche attends among the intimate circle, and reads aloud his own essay in celebration, though Wagner's mood on the day is darkly pessimistic rather than triumphant. The professor of philology is now publicly, dangerously, a Wagnerian; his academic colleagues at Basel look on with growing unease.
suggested_refs: The Bayreuth Festspielhaus foundation-stone ceremony, 1872

stops.name: Bayreuth, the first Festival, the base and the predictable
stops.campa: The Festspielhaus opens at last on the thirteenth of August with the first complete Ring cycle, an event four years and a fortune in the making, attended by an emperor and the cultivated Europe of the day. Nietzsche is present, but where he had once looked for a rebirth of tragic culture he now sees only fashionable crowds, a bourgeois circus around his former idol. He leaves partway through the festival for the quiet of the Bohemian forest, the first visible crack in the worship of eight years.
suggested_refs: Bayreuth Festspielhaus, opening night program, 13 August 1876

stops.name: Sorrento, Villa Rubinacci, Malwida's household of free spirits
stops.campa: Broken in health and disillusioned by Bayreuth, Nietzsche accepts leave from Basel and travels south to Sorrento, to the Villa Rubinacci, as the guest of Malwida von Meysenbug, who mothers a small household of free spirits: Paul Rée, young Albert Brenner, and himself. Through the winter and into May he walks the cliffs above the bay, drafts what will become Human, All Too Human, and later calls these months among the happiest of his troubled life. Free-thought, not devotion, is now the household's true religion.
suggested_refs: Villa Rubinacci (Pensione Allemande), Sorrento
Malwida von Meysenbug's memoirs

stops.name: Basel: Human, All Too Human crosses Parsifal in the post
stops.campa: Nietzsche sends Wagner an inscribed copy of Human, All Too Human just as Wagner sends him the text of Parsifal; the two packages cross in the mail like two swords. Wagner, remaking his own myth into a drama of Christian redemption, cannot forgive the book's cool, aphoristic dismantling of the metaphysical comforts they once shared. Nietzsche calls Parsifal 'much too religious for me, bound as I am to the Greek and human.' No further letters of friendship pass between them; the god that made him is now the idol he must break.
stops.quote: Impressions after the first reading: more Liszt than Wagner, spirit of the counter-revolution. The whole thing is much too religious for me, bound as I am to the Greek and human.
stops.quote_source: Notebook entry on receiving the Parsifal libretto, 1878
suggested_refs: Wagner's Parsifal libretto, presentation copy, 1878
Human, All Too Human, first edition, 1878

stops.name: Basel, the resignation, the pension, the wanderer begins
stops.campa: Migraines, near-blindness, and violent stomach attacks have made teaching impossible; after ten years in the chair Ritschl won for him, Nietzsche resigns from Basel with a small pension and no fixed post ever again. He is thirty-four, unemployed by choice of health, and about to become the wandering figure of legend: no wife, no home, no university, only a trunk, a green eyeshade against the light, and the mountain and seaside boarding-houses of Switzerland and Italy for the next decade.
suggested_refs: Nietzsche's resignation letter to the Basel curatorium, 1879

segments.name: Venice, Genoa, and the Rock at Surlej

stops.name: Venice, the Riva, Peter Gast, the first cohabitation
stops.campa: Nietzsche spends four months of the year in Venice and nearby Riva, sharing rooms with his devoted young disciple Heinrich Köselitz, whom he has renamed Peter Gast: 'guest,' fittingly, since the young musician will spend decades transcribing Nietzsche's ruined handwriting and correcting his proofs for love of him alone. The lagoon city's light and its gondoliers' cries enter Nietzsche's ear as music; he will later say Venice, more than any place, taught him what the word 'music' should mean.
stops.quote: When I seek another word for music I never find any other word than Venice.
stops.quote_source: Ecce Homo, "Why I Am So Clever," §7
suggested_refs: Peter Gast's manuscript transcriptions of Nietzsche's notebooks

stops.name: Genoa, Salita delle Battistine, the garret of 164 steps
stops.campa: Nietzsche discovers Genoa and takes a mansard room at Salita delle Battistine 8, up a hundred and sixty-four steps, for eighty lire a month: a view over the harbor's masts and the Ligurian sea bought with a punishing climb his ruined body barely survives. Here, between headaches, he composes pages of Daybreak and later of Zarathustra itself, calling the city's steep light and hard stone streets a tonic for a soul that needs stone to lean against.
stops.quote: To reach my little room under the roof, I must climb a hundred and sixty-four steps.
suggested_refs: The house at Salita delle Battistine 8, Genoa

stops.name: Sils-Maria, Surlej, the pyramidal rock, the thought of thoughts
stops.campa: Walking the woods beside Lake Silvaplana near the hamlet of Surlej, six thousand feet above the sea, Nietzsche stops beside a mighty pyramidal block of granite by the waterfall, and the thought of eternal recurrence, as he will later say, overtakes him like a flash of lightning, the highest formula of affirmation a mind can bear: that this life, exactly as it is, returns without end, and must be willed as if it would. He scrawls on a sheet of paper the date and the words '6000 feet above sea level and much higher above all human things.' Zarathustra is already walking toward him.
stops.quote: 6000 feet above sea level and much higher above all human things.
stops.quote_source: Notebook fragment, Sils-Maria, August 1881 (cf. Ecce Homo)
suggested_refs: The Nietzsche-Stein (Zarathustra-Stein) at Surlej, Lake Silvaplana
Zoroaster's own revelation at the river-ford, for comparison of the two prophets of eternal fire

stops.name: Genoa, the sun of Die fröhliche Wissenschaft
stops.campa: Back in the garret above the harbor for a second Genoese winter, buoyed by the vision at Surlej, Nietzsche completes The Gay Science, the most sun-drenched of his books, closing it with the first announcement of Zarathustra's descent from the mountain. He proclaims in its pages that God is dead, and that this death is less a catastrophe than a horizon suddenly thrown open: a dangerous, exhilarating freedom that only the strongest spirits can bear without falling into nihilism's abyss.
stops.quote: God is dead; but given the way of men, there may still be caves for thousands of years in which his shadow will be shown.
suggested_refs: First edition of Die fröhliche Wissenschaft, 1882

stops.name: Rome, St. Peter's, Lou von Salomé
stops.campa: Introduced by Malwida von Meysenbug, Nietzsche meets the brilliant twenty-one-year-old Russian, Lou von Salomé, inside St. Peter's Basilica itself. He is thirty-seven and instantly, uncharacteristically smitten by an intellect he judges nearly his equal; within days he has Paul Rée carry a proposal of marriage to her on his behalf, not knowing Rée has already proposed himself. Lou refuses both men but accepts a stranger, still more dangerous, arrangement: a working trinity of minds, unchaperoned travel, philosophy without love's usual claims.
suggested_refs: St. Peter's Basilica, Rome
Lou von Salomé's photographs with Nietzsche and Rée, the cart-and-whip photograph

stops.name: Orta, Monte Sacro, the exquisite dream
stops.campa: Alone together at last, Nietzsche and Lou climb the Sacro Monte above the island-studded Lake Orta, through the chapels of the pilgrim's way to its summit view. He calls the ascent afterward the most exquisite dream of his life, and writes to her soon after that at Orta he first conceived a plan to lead her, step by careful step, to the final consequence of his philosophy, she the first person he has judged fit to receive it entire. No third person, this once, stands between them on the mountain.
stops.quote: Back at Orta, I conceived a plan of leading you step by step to the final consequence of my philosophy — you as the first person I took to be fit for this.
suggested_refs: Sacro Monte di Orta, the pilgrim chapels above Lake Orta

stops.name: Tautenburg, the philosophical trio, Elisabeth's watch
stops.campa: For three weeks in the forest village of Tautenburg near Jena, Nietzsche and Lou talk philosophy for hours daily under the chaperonage, and increasingly the jealous surveillance, of his sister Elisabeth, who despises the freethinking Russian and works from the first day to destroy the friendship. The talks are the most sustained intellectual companionship of Nietzsche's life; within months, poisoned by Elisabeth's letters and his own wounded pride, the whole trio, Lou, Rée, and Nietzsche, will have broken apart in mutual recrimination.
suggested_refs: Tautenburg forest lodgings, near Dornburg

segments.name: Rapallo and the Birth of Zarathustra

stops.name: Rapallo, ten lucid days, Zarathustra Part One
stops.campa: Wintering on the little gulf of Rapallo near Genoa, heartbroken over Lou and grieving news that will soon arrive of Wagner's death in Venice, Nietzsche writes the whole of Thus Spoke Zarathustra's first part in a single ten-day eruption of composition, walking the coastal paths toward Zoagli and Portofino as the sentences arrive whole, unbidden, faster than his hand can set them down. He will later say Zarathustra himself came upon him on these walks, not that he sought Zarathustra out. He has never experienced, he writes to Peter Gast, such a winter.
stops.quote: I have had ten absolutely lucid and exuberant days — I have never experienced such a winter.
suggested_refs: The coastal path from Rapallo to Zoagli, "Nietzsche's walk"
Manuscript of Also sprach Zarathustra, Part One

stops.name: Sils-Maria, Zarathustra Part Two, six weeks
stops.campa: Returning for the summer to his rented room in the Durisch house at Sils-Maria, the same Engadine village whose rock had given him the eternal return, Nietzsche writes the second part of Zarathustra in a comparable burst, some six or seven weeks of walking, notebook in hand, along the lakeside paths he now knows like scripture. The mountain air he credits, more than any doctor, with keeping him alive at all; the small room above the Durisch family's grocery becomes the summer study from which four more years of the Engadine visits will follow.
suggested_refs: The Nietzsche-Haus, Sils-Maria (the Durisch house), Via da Marias 67

stops.name: Nice, rue Ségurane, Zarathustra Part Three
stops.campa: The first of what will be five winters in Nice, in a rented room on the rue Ségurane and later the Pension de Genève, gives Nietzsche the mild sea-light his health now requires and the long solitary walks toward Mont Boron and along the corniche path to Èze, a route the town will one day rename in his honor. Here in January he completes the third part of Zarathustra, the most severe and vertiginous of the four, closing on the vision of the eternal return set now fully into Zarathustra's own mouth.
suggested_refs: The "Chemin de Nietzsche" (Nietzsche's Path) between Èze and Nice

stops.name: Venice, Gast's empty apartment, the proofs
stops.campa: While Peter Gast is elsewhere trying vainly to get his own opera staged, Nietzsche occupies his friend's empty Venetian apartment for weeks, correcting proofs of Zarathustra and letting the city's canals and bells stand in for the companionship Gast cannot presently give. Increasingly it is Gast, more than any philosopher or lover, who reads Nietzsche's ruined handwriting, copies his manuscripts fair, and argues the publishers into printing books almost no one yet wants to buy.
suggested_refs: Peter Gast's Venetian apartment
Fair-copy manuscripts of Zarathustra in Gast's hand

stops.name: Nice, Zarathustra Part Four, forty copies for friends
stops.campa: No publisher will touch a fourth part of a book selling almost nothing; Nietzsche pays out of his own thin pension to have forty copies of Zarathustra Part Four privately printed, and sends them only to the handful of friends he thinks capable of understanding it: Overbeck, Gast, Burckhardt, Rohde among them. The greatest work he believes he has written, or ever will write, exists for now as a private pamphlet passed hand to hand among a dozen readers, unread by the world it addresses.
stops.quote: I have given mankind the profoundest book it possesses, my Zarathustra: I shall shortly give it the most independent one.
stops.quote_source: Twilight of the Idols, "Skirmishes of an Untimely Man," §51
suggested_refs: One of the forty privately printed copies of Also sprach Zarathustra, Part Four, 1885

segments.name: Nice, Genoa, Venice: The Last Books

stops.name: Nice, Beyond Good and Evil completed
stops.campa: In the winter light of Nice, still walking the same corniche paths, Nietzsche finishes Beyond Good and Evil, the systematic prelude he says Zarathustra's poetry required: a book that names the coming philosophers of the future, dissects the slave-morality of Christian Europe, and diagnoses the herd instinct with a scalpel's coldness. Self-published as Zarathustra was, at his own expense, it sells scarcely better; the isolation of the wandering years is now total, but the sentences arrive with undiminished, almost frightening, clarity.
suggested_refs: First edition of Jenseits von Gut und Böse, 1886

stops.name: Venice, the last visit, the Genealogy's proofs
stops.campa: Nietzsche comes to Venice for what will prove his final visit, working through the evening of the twenty-first of September on the proofs of On the Genealogy of Morals and sending out his newly composed Hymn to Life for Gast to set to music. He does not know it is a last farewell to the lagoon whose bells taught him what music should mean; within a year Turin, not Venice, will become his final address, and within fifteen months his mind itself will be gone.
suggested_refs: On the Genealogy of Morals, proof sheets, 1887
Nietzsche's Hymnus an das Leben, score by Peter Gast

stops.name: Turin, the discovery of the city, the Alps in the window
stops.campa: Returning to the city he had briefly sampled in the spring, Nietzsche takes rooms on the fourth floor of Via Carlo Alberto 6, above the arcades of the Galleria Subalpina, and declares Turin the discovery of his life: its royal arcades, its clear autumn air, the snow-Alps visible at the end of every straight avenue. He calls it the first city he has found truly fit for him. In this apartment, in an extraordinary final burst, he will write four books in as many months.
stops.quote: This is decidedly the place for me... I feel that I have discovered the town made for me.
suggested_refs: Via Carlo Alberto 6, Turin, Nietzsche's last apartment
The Galleria Subalpina, Turin

stops.name: Turin, Ecce Homo, Twilight of the Idols, "I am dynamite"
stops.campa: In a white heat of productivity that his friends will later read as the first sign of collapse, Nietzsche completes Twilight of the Idols, The Case of Wagner, Nietzsche contra Wagner, and the strange, self-glorifying autobiography Ecce Homo, all within these Turin months. Its chapter titles alone announce a mind approaching its own myth from the inside: 'Why I Am So Wise,' 'Why I Am So Clever,' 'Why I Write Such Good Books.' He calls himself, without irony now, no longer a man but a piece of destiny.
stops.quote: I am no man, I am dynamite.
stops.quote_source: Ecce Homo, "Why I Am a Destiny," §1
suggested_refs: Manuscript of Ecce Homo, Turin, 1888

segments.name: Turin, the Collapse, and the Long Dusk

stops.name: Turin, Piazza Carlo Alberto, the horse and the letters
stops.campa: On the morning of the third of January, walking out from Via Carlo Alberto, Nietzsche comes upon a cab-horse flogged by its driver in the piazza and, the canon holds, flings his arms about its neck to shield it before collapsing to the pavement. He is carried home, and does not truly rise again as himself. Within days a burst of terse, luminous, deranged notes goes out over his signature: 'Dionysus' to Cosima Wagner, 'Ariadne, I love you'; to Jacob Burckhardt, that he would rather be a Basel professor than God, but has not carried private egoism so far as to skip creating the world on his own account.
stops.quote: Actually, I would much rather be a Basle professor than God; but I have not ventured to carry my private egoism so far as to omit creating the world on his account.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Jacob Burckhardt, early January 1889
suggested_refs: Piazza Carlo Alberto, Turin
The 'Wahnbriefe' (madness letters), January 1889, Nietzsche archive

stops.name: Basel, Overbeck, the Friedmatt asylum
stops.campa: Alarmed by the letters, Nietzsche's old friend and colleague Franz Overbeck travels at once to Turin, finds him raving and playing the piano with his elbows for the landlord, and brings him back by train to Basel, where he is admitted to the Friedmatt psychiatric clinic on the tenth of January. Overbeck will say of that journey only that the Nietzsche he had known was no more. The scholar of Dionysus is now, in medical fact, a committed patient.
suggested_refs: Franz Overbeck's account of the Turin journey, January 1889

stops.name: Jena, Binswanger's clinic, dementia paralytica
stops.campa: His mother Franziska moves him from Basel to the university psychiatric clinic at Jena, under Otto Binswanger, a specialist in general paralysis of the insane; the admission record reads simply 'type of illness: paralytic mental illness.' He remains here more than a year, sometimes lucid enough to play the piano beautifully, more often confused, occasionally violent, cared for now as a body and a name rather than as the mind that wrote Zarathustra, that mind already, by his own earlier riddle, having died with his father decades before.
suggested_refs: Binswanger's clinical case notes on Nietzsche, Jena, 1889-90

stops.name: Naumburg, Weingarten 18, the mother's watch
stops.campa: Released from Jena, Nietzsche is brought home to the house at Weingarten 18 in Naumburg, the same house of women he left as a young graduate for Bonn; his mother nurses him now as she once nursed his father's dying, feeding him, walking him, enduring his rages and his silences for seven years. In 1894 his sister Elisabeth, returned from her failed colony in Paraguay, founds the Nietzsche-Archiv in this same house, already shaping, before her brother's death, the myth that will outlast and distort him.
suggested_refs: Nietzsche-Haus, Weingarten 18, Naumburg, and the founding of the Nietzsche-Archiv, 1894

stops.name: Naumburg, Steiner in the sickroom
stops.campa: Elisabeth, who has engaged the young Austrian scholar Rudolf Steiner to help order her brother's library and papers, leads him up to the darkened sickroom at Weingarten. On a couch lies Nietzsche, mad these seven years, gazing without seeing; Steiner will later write that he beheld the philosopher's soul already hovering above the sick head, radiant, loosed from a body that in life it could never truly inhabit, an image Steiner carries into his own book on Nietzsche as the fighter for freedom against his age. Nietzsche himself, present in the room, is absent from the meeting entirely.
suggested_refs: Hans Olde's drawings of the dying Nietzsche, Naumburg, 1899
Rudolf Steiner, Friedrich Nietzsche: Fighter for Freedom (1895)

stops.name: Weimar, Villa Silberblick, the archive founded
stops.campa: Their mother Franziska dies in April 1897; within months Elisabeth, with money from the wealthy friend Meta von Salis, secures the Villa Silberblick above Weimar's Ilm valley and moves her brother there, the Nietzsche-Archiv following him from Naumburg into its new rooms. It is, by the strangest coincidence the canon can offer, the same small city where, in these very years, Rudolf Steiner works seven quiet years cataloguing Goethe's scientific manuscripts in the Goethe-Schiller-Archiv barely a mile across the Ilm, the sickbed and the archive-worker briefly sharing one town without ever again meeting.
suggested_refs: Villa Silberblick, Humboldtstraße 36, Weimar
The Goethe-Schiller-Archiv, Weimar, where Steiner worked 1890-1897

stops.name: Weimar, the last silence, death
stops.campa: For three more years Nietzsche lies in the Villa Silberblick, paralyzed by strokes, mute, cared for by his sister and by nurses while his fame, unknown to him, begins at last to spread across Europe through the very books written in solitude and contempt for popularity. He dies on the twenty-fifth of August 1900, of pneumonia following a stroke, not quite fifty-six years old: as my father I am already dead, he had written at the very start; as my mother I lived and grew old; now both halves of the riddle close together in the same year's end.
stops.quote: There lay Nietzsche upon a couch... with the beautiful forehead, the forehead of an artist and a thinker in one.
stops.quote_source: Rudolf Steiner, recalling the Naumburg sickroom, in Mein Lebensgang (GA 28), ch. XVIII
